head:
Method · Field tests

Testing your fitness at home: what equipment changes

A chair, a stopwatch, a watch on your wrist, a gym: each tool gives you a number. They are not worth the same. This article takes them one by one, from the simplest to the most equipped, to tell you what each one really measures, how accurately, and which one to choose.

The questionIf you don't have a laboratory, what is the test you do at home worth?

You want to know where you stand. Maybe you are getting back into exercise, maybe you already train and want a reference point. Either way, you face the same choice. You can use nothing and count chair stands. You can take out a stopwatch and run or walk for a set time. You can look at the “VO2max” your watch displays without you having asked for anything. You can go to the gym and lift a maximal load.

The reference lies elsewhere. For cardiorespiratory fitness, it is a laboratory test with a mask that analyses the air you breathe, on a treadmill or bike, until exhaustion. Almost nobody has regular access to it. Everything you do at home is therefore an estimate, and an estimate can be good, mediocre, or good only for some people.

What interests me here is the question that comes before any norm table: before comparing yourself to a norm, does the number you get mean anything, and does that depend on what you have in your hands?

The question

When you test your fitness at home, what changes depending on the equipment (nothing, a stopwatch, a watch, a gym): how reliable the result is, what it really tells you, and what you can do with it?

What's at stakeThe wrong tool leads you to the wrong decision

A fitness test is used to make decisions, and each tool can mislead you in a different way. What follows checks, tool by tool, what the equipment brings: first what a test must prove, then four levels of equipment, from the simplest to the most equipped, then the shared limits.

The first decision is whether you can get started. Many beginners believe they need equipment to get a serious starting point. If a chair and a stopwatch are enough, that barrier falls. Conversely, a watch figure that tells you “low” when it is wrong can discourage you for no reason, and a flattering figure can give you a false sense of security.

The second decision is whether you are progressing. Training lasts weeks. To judge that it works, a test repeated a month later has to be comparable with the first. A tool that is precise in absolute value but unstable from one day to the next is useless for this. A tool that is imprecise in absolute value but very stable can be excellent for tracking yourself.

The third decision is about safety. A test where you push your body to its maximum is not trivial if you have, without knowing it, a heart or lung problem. Choosing your test also means choosing the level of effort you expose yourself to, and knowing which signs mean you should stop.

Step 1 of 6A good test has to pass four tests

Before comparing the tools, you need a grid. Researchers judge a field test with four criteria, and they do not say the same thing.

  1. Validity.Does the result agree with the reference measurement? It is often expressed as a correlation coefficient, written r, between 0 (no link) and 1 (perfect link). An r of 0.8 means the two measures rank people in roughly the same order, not that they give the same value.
  2. Reliability.If you repeat the test under the same conditions, do you get the same result? It is measured by an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) or by a typical error, in the units of the test (metres, repetitions).
  3. Accessibility.Does it need space, equipment, a partner, medical advice? A test you cannot repeat regularly will not track you.
  4. Limits.Who was the test validated for? Many results come from older people, patients or elite athletes, not necessarily from you.

One distinction matters right away: a test can be reliable without being valid. A scale that always shows 5 kg too much is perfectly reliable and completely wrong in absolute value. It remains very useful if you only want to know whether your weight is moving. For a fitness test, the logic is the same. If your goal is to track yourself, reliability matters more than absolute validity. If your goal is to place yourself relative to others, it is the opposite.

Field tests never measure VO2max directly: a meta-analysis on the 20-metre shuttle run calls it “an estimate, not a direct measurement”.5 This applies to all the tools that follow, starting with the simplest.

Step 2 of 6With nothing: a chair is enough to measure leg strength, with good reliability

The best-documented test in what I was able to read is the 30-second chair stand. You sit in the middle of a straight chair without armrests, about 43 to 46 cm high, arms crossed over your chest, feet flat. For 30 seconds you stand up fully and then sit back down, touching the seat, as many times as possible. A repetition where you push with your arms or do not stand fully upright does not count.8 You need a chair, a phone stopwatch, and two minutes.

This test mainly measures leg strength and endurance, not cardio: it does not replace an endurance test.

Is it valid?

In the founding study by Jones and colleagues, in 76 older adults living at home, the number of stands has a correlation of 0.77 with the strength measured on the leg press, relative to body weight.7 It is a strong link, though not a perfect one: the test ranks people well by leg strength, but two people with the same score do not have exactly the same strength.

Is it reliable?

Yes. The same group found an r of 0.89 between two attempts, and other teams found coefficients of 0.97 to 0.98 in people with hip or knee osteoarthritis, and 0.98 in 26 obese older adults.7,9 When the test is done the same way, with the same chair, it gives almost the same number.

The number of chair stands in 30 seconds drops markedly after age 60

Means from McKay et al. (2017), 988 people aged 3 to 94, as reported by the SRALab database. The standard deviations are 5 to 6 stands: individuals are spread widely around these means.7

What this means

The test shows a drop in the means of about 6 to 7 stands between 20 to 59 years and 60 years and over, in men and women alike. This tells you two things: the same score does not mean the same at 25 and at 65, and you need a norm table by age and sex. The standard deviations of 5 to 6 stands also show that being below the mean is very common and does not signal anything abnormal.

For older people, the norms published by Rikli and Jones go further than the mean: they give the number of stands that corresponds to maintaining independence. For ages 60 to 64, 15 stands for women and 17 for men, and 9 for both sexes at ages 90 to 94.7 This is not a performance target, it is a threshold below which daily life (getting up from an armchair, a toilet, a staircase) becomes harder.

And push-ups, the plank, the Ruffier test, the Harvard step test?

Push-ups and the plank measure upper-body and trunk strength and endurance. The Ruffier and Harvard tests measure how your heart rate rises and then falls after a short, standardised effort.

I give no coefficient for them: I was not able to read a reliable one and I do not quote a figure from memory. The grid applies: same conditions, same technique, and compare yourself with yourself.

For endurance, you need a stopwatch and some space.

Step 3 of 6With a stopwatch: endurance is finally measured, but the first attempt is the weakest

Three tests use a stopwatch and space: the Cooper test (running as far as possible in 12 minutes), the 6-minute walk and the 20-metre shuttle run (running between two lines at a speed that increases, until you can no longer keep up). All three estimate your endurance from a distance or a stage.

The Cooper test: very stable, validity not verified here

A reliability study had 15 recreational runners, 34.5 years old on average, do the test twice on a 400 m track, 48 hours apart. The ICC for the distance covered is 0.99.6 The typical error from one attempt to the next is 52.2 m, or 1.7% of the distance. The authors draw a simple rule from this: a difference of less than 52 metres should not be attributed to training or detraining.

This study did not compare the Cooper test with VO2max measured in the laboratory: its validity is not demonstrated by this source, and the sample is small (15 trained men).

The 20-metre shuttle run: moderate to good validity, across many studies

A meta-analysis pooled 57 studies and 78 correlation values between the shuttle run score and measured VO2max. The correlations range from 0.66 to 0.84, and rise from 0.78 to 0.95 when sex, age or body mass are added to the formula.5 In plain terms: the shuttle run ranks people rather well by VO2max, but it leaves a margin, and the authors specify that the score remains “an estimate”.

The 6-minute walk: accessible, with a learning effect

You walk at your own pace, as far as possible without running, along a flat 30 m corridor, for 6 minutes, and you measure the distance. The American Thoracic Society (ATS) text describes a test designed for patients and for the clinic. It states that this test does not determine peak VO2; it is complementary to an exercise test. In patients with end-stage lung disease, it reports a correlation of 0.73 between the distance and peak VO2.10 This is not your population, but it gives the order of magnitude.

The most useful point for you is the learning effect. A study of 46 adults (intellectual disability, 41 years old on average) had the test repeated three times.12

The second attempt is better than the first, then the result stabilises

Source: Guerra-Balic et al., Research in Developmental Disabilities, 2015 (46 adults with intellectual disability, abstract). Attempt 1 differs from 2 and 3 (p < 0.001), but 2 does not differ from 3. +29.1 m = 489.4 − 460.3, or about 6.3%, a calculated (derived) figure.12

What this means

The first attempt underestimates what you are capable of, by about 6% in this study. After that, the result stabilises: the ICC between attempts 2 and 3 is 0.96. The ATS text gives a similar range (0 to 17% better on the second test) and indicates that performance generally stabilises after two tests.10,11 The first attempt is a trial run: do not use it as your starting point, and count a change only if it exceeds the typical error (about 52 m for the Cooper test).

That leaves the watch, which estimates your VO2max without a dedicated test. What are these numbers worth?

Step 4 of 6With a watch: a group's average is acceptable, your own number can be far from reality

Watches display an estimated VO2max. Studies compare them with a laboratory measurement.

The 2022 review

Molina-Garcia and colleagues (INTERLIVE network) gathered 14 validation studies of watches and wristbands. They separate two families of algorithms. Watches that rely on resting information (age, weight, resting heart rate) overestimate VO2max on average by 2.17 ml/kg/min, with limits of agreement from −13.07 to +17.41. Those that rely on exercise data have a mean bias of only −0.09, with limits from −9.92 to +9.74.1 The authors' conclusion: estimates from exercise are suitable at the level of a population, but the individual error remains large.

The “limits of agreement” are the zone where 95% of the differences between the watch and the laboratory fall. A bias close to zero means that, across the group, the watch does not err in one direction more than the other. Wide limits mean that, for a given person, the difference can be large. Worked example, not a study result: with limits of about ±10, a real VO2max of 40 can show up as 30 as well as 50.

Watches are off by 4 to 13% on average depending on the study and the group

Apple Watch: conference abstract, 30 active adults, 5 to 10 days of wear then a maximal treadmill test. Garmin Forerunner 245: Engel et al., Eur J Appl Physiol, 2025, first of two attempts (35 athletes, mean VO2max of 60.1 ml/kg/min). Different studies, different devices: this is not a ranking of brands.2,3

What this means

An error of 13% means that, for a real VO2max of 40, the watch is on average off by plus or minus 5. The Garmin's error goes from 4.1% in moderately trained athletes to 10.4% in highly trained ones: the watch underestimates more the higher the level. The accuracy of your own number therefore depends on your level.

Details of the Garmin study

The 35 athletes ran twice for 15 minutes outdoors with the watch, then did a maximal treadmill test with gas analysis.2,14 On the first attempt, the watch underestimates by 4.73 ml/kg/min on average, with limits of agreement from −12.78 to +3.32. The bias is −2.17 in the moderately trained and −6.88 in the highly trained; the agreement (ICC) falls from 0.63 to 0.34, which is poor.2 The authors conclude that the estimate is valid in the moderately trained, less so in the highly trained, and that the laboratory remains preferable for accuracy.

And the Apple Watch?

In the conference abstract cited, the watch underestimates on average by 5.51 ml/kg/min (limits of agreement from −7.27 to 18.30), with a mean absolute error of 13.14%. Heart rate, however, is very close to that of a chest strap: a difference of 1.1 beats per minute on average. The authors judge that the estimated VO2max is not yet usable in the clinic. A small study (16 volunteers, Series 5) found similar means (37.7 versus 39.9) but a correlation of 0.2 between individual values.3,13 It comes from a university repository: a signal, not proof.

The error zone of an individual measurement is wide, and it differs by method

Calculated (derived) figures: width = upper limit minus lower limit of the published limits of agreement (for example 17.41 − (−13.07) = 30.48). The direction of the bias sign differs from one study to another: only the width is comparable.1,2,3

What this means

Even in the best case (exercise-based algorithm), the zone in which your individual number can fall spans nearly 20 ml/kg/min. In other words, the error zone is wider than many of the gaps between two fitness levels that you would want to tell apart. To place yourself, it is too wide. To track yourself over time, the trend could remain useful, but I have not read a study that demonstrates it.

One point is reassuring: heart rate at the wrist is well measured. A study by Düking and colleagues on 25 participants and four watches (Apple Watch Series 4, Polar Vantage V, Garmin Fenix 5, Fitbit Versa) ranked the Apple Watch first for heart rate, followed by the Polar, the Garmin and then the Fitbit, and judged the Polar and the Apple suitable.4 One point is a warning: the same study judges that none of the four is suitable for measuring energy expenditure (calories). This study does not concern VO2max.

Step 5 of 6With a gym: a more direct measure of strength, but one I cannot put a number on here, and a higher risk

The gym adds two classic tests. The 1RM (one-repetition maximum) is the heaviest load you can lift a single time with good technique, on a movement such as the squat or the bench press. The grip dynamometer measures, in kilos, the strength of your hand when you squeeze the device as hard as possible.

These two tests measure strength, not cardio, and they measure it directly instead of estimating it from another signal (a common-sense argument, not a study result).

I give no coefficient for the 1RM or for the dynamometer: I was not able to read a reliable one, and I do not quote a figure from memory. Without a figure, I can talk about risk. The 1RM requires solid technique, a progressive warm-up and, for risky movements, someone to spot you. A technique error under maximal load can cause injury, which is not the case with a chair stand. The dynamometer requires a brief effort, but you need to have access to one.

What this means

The gym does not give you a better cardio test. It gives you more direct strength measures. If you are a beginner, the gain over the chair stand is not demonstrated here, and the safety cost is higher. Do a 1RM with supervision; without it, a light-load strength-endurance test is safer.

What equipment does not fix: day-to-day variation

Whatever the tool, part of the difference between two attempts is noise. For the chair stand, the smallest change that exceeds measurement error (minimal detectable change) ranges from 1.64 to 2.79 stands, depending on the groups studied, all with osteoarthritis.8 For the Cooper test, it is about 52 m.6 These values come from populations different from yours, but they give the order of magnitude: if your score moves by 1 stand or 20 m, you cannot conclude anything.

Safety

Fitness tests push your body. The clinical texts on walk tests, written for patients and carers, give criteria that help you identify who should ask for medical advice beforehand.

Absolute contraindications for the 6-minute walk: unstable angina, a heart attack in the previous month. Relative contraindications: resting heart rate above 120, systolic pressure above 180 mmHg, diastolic pressure above 100 mmHg.10 The European and American statement lists more (rhythm disorders, syncope, uncontrolled heart failure or asthma, acute illness).11

Stop the test immediately if you have:

  • chest pain;
  • intolerable breathlessness;
  • leg cramps;
  • staggering;
  • excessive sweating;
  • a pale or grey complexion.

If you have a known heart or lung disease, are on treatment, have pain or breathlessness on exertion, or are returning after a long period without activity, ask for medical advice before doing a maximal test. Complications are rare: among 741 rehabilitation patients, 6% had an adverse event, most often a drop in oxygenation that led to the test being stopped.11 These are patients, but it confirms that stopping in time is the rule.

Step 6 of 6Side by side, and facing the objections: what the numbers allow, and what they do not

The link with the reference is strong for simple tests, highly variable for watches

The bars show the 95% confidence interval (CI) (chair, Garmin) or the range of reported correlations (shuttle run). The dots show the central value. Correlation (r) and ICC are not the same measure, and the populations differ (older people, patients, athletes, healthy adults): the chart gives orders of magnitude, it does not rank the tests. No validity value was read for the Cooper test, nor for push-ups, the plank, the Ruffier, the Harvard, the 1RM and the dynamometer.1,2,5,7,10,13

What this means

Tests without a sensor and with a stopwatch show links of 0.66 to 0.84 with their reference, on samples counted in tens of studies (shuttle run) or tens of people (chair). Watches, on samples of 16 to 35 people, range from 0.2 to 0.71, with confidence intervals that stretch almost from 0 to 1. In plain terms: we know that the chair stand and the shuttle run measure well what they aim at, and we cannot yet say the same with certainty of a watch for a given person.

Objection 1: “Newer equipment must be more accurate”

In the meta-analysis, the difference in error comes from the type of algorithm: estimates based on exercise data have a lower bias than those based on rest.1 Even the best family leaves an individual error zone about 20 ml/kg/min wide. The authors note that these methods still need to be improved; nothing says that a newer watch does better.

Objection 2: “These norms come from older or sick people, not from me”

That is correct, and it is the main limit of this article. The chair stand coefficients come from older people and patients with osteoarthritis, those for the walk from patients and adults with intellectual disability, those for the Cooper test from 15 runners. What probably carries over: the reliability of well-standardised protocols. What carries over less: the norm tables and the independence thresholds.

Objection 3: “An imprecise test is useless”

It depends on what you expect from it. To place yourself, a test with a wide error is no use: that is the case of a watch for a single person. To track yourself, what matters is stability, excellent for the Cooper test (0.99) and for the 6-minute walk after a first attempt (0.96).

What remains uncertain

I have no evidence read for push-ups, the plank, the Ruffier, the Harvard, the 1RM and the dynamometer, nor a study comparing the Cooper test with VO2max, nor a study showing that a watch's trend is reliable from one week to the next. These are open questions, not negative answers.

The answerEquipment mainly changes accuracy and risk, not whether you can test yourself

Your question was: what changes depending on the equipment? Here is the answer, with its level of certainty.

Solid. Simple tests, with a strict protocol, are reliable: the chair stand (0.89 to 0.98 depending on the studies), the Cooper test (0.99), the 6-minute walk after a first attempt (0.96). When you repeat them under the same conditions, you get almost the same result. Correlations with the reference exist and are moderate to good for the chair stand (0.77 with leg strength) and the shuttle run (0.66 to 0.84 with VO2max). The 6-minute walk has a learning effect: the first attempt is lower.

Probable. To track yourself, a simple test, repeated under the same conditions, is at least as useful as a watch. This is the logical consequence of the reliability and measurement error figures, not a direct comparison read in a study.

Not demonstrated or fragile. The individual accuracy of watches: the group average is acceptable, your own number can be off by several ml/kg/min, and the error is larger in the highly trained. The validity of the Cooper test against VO2max in the sources read, and that of all the tests I was not able to document.

Equipment therefore changes absolute accuracy (from the chair, which does not estimate cardio, to the watch, which estimates it with a wide error zone), accessibility and risk (the 1RM is the most exposed). It does not change the logic of tracking: standardise well, repeat, compare with yourself. You don't need equipment to know where you stand.

What we put in placeChoose your test, do it well, repeat it

What follows is an editorial approach based on the figures above. The recommended frequencies are practical recommendations, not study results.

  1. Choose according to your question, not according to your equipment.Leg strength: 30 s chair stand. Endurance: Cooper test, 6-minute walk or shuttle run, depending on your level and your space. A strength test in the gym only if you have experience and supervision. The watch as a complement, never alone.
  2. Do a trial run.Especially for the 6-minute walk, where the first attempt underestimates by about 6% in the study read. The second is your real starting point.
  3. Standardise.Same chair (43 to 46 cm), same surface, same time of day, same warm-up, same instructions. Write them down so you can reproduce them. Without this, you are measuring noise.
  4. Keep your test's margin in mind.Less than 2 to 3 stands for the chair stand (osteoarthritis values, as an order of magnitude), less than 52 m for the Cooper test: this is not a real change.
  5. Repeat the test every 4 to 8 weeks.This rhythm is a practical recommendation: long enough for training to have an effect, short enough to correct course. Do not chain it with a hard session the day before.
  6. Use your watch for the trend, not for the verdict.If you have doubts about the number, do not take it as a diagnosis. No watch figure should make you decide to stop or to push harder.

The THW test on the page, just below, gives you the exact protocol to follow. What the article helps you decide is what to do it with, how often to repeat it, and how much weight to give the result. If you are a beginner, remember this above all: a simple test, done well, repeated regularly, is worth more than a watch figure you trust without knowing how far.

What these figures do not say
  • Most of the coefficients come from populations that are not yours: older people, patients with osteoarthritis, lung patients, adults with intellectual disability, endurance athletes.
  • Several results come from small samples (15 runners, 16 adults, 26 older adults, 35 athletes).
  • Watches change algorithm and software: a study on one model does not hold for the next.
  • Push-ups, the plank, the Ruffier, the Harvard, the 1RM and the dynamometer are not quantified here for lack of a source read.
  • The independence norms for the chair stand concern people aged 60 and over.

Frequently asked questions

I'm a beginner, which test should I start with?

With the 30-second chair stand: it needs a chair and a stopwatch, takes two minutes and has good reliability figures. If you also want an endurance reference point, the 6-minute walk with a trial first attempt is the gentlest of the three timed tests.7,10

My watch shows a low VO2max: should I worry?

Not from that number alone. The individual error can reach several ml/kg/min, and the error zone covers nearly 20 ml/kg/min in total in the best case. Repeat a simple test, and talk to a doctor if you have symptoms on exertion.1,3

Do I need to buy equipment to test myself better?

The studies read do not show that more expensive equipment gives you a better starting point. They rather show that rigour of method (same conditions, trial first attempt) matters more than the tool.1,6,12

The first result is bad: is that final?

No, especially for the 6-minute walk, where the first attempt is about 6% lower than the following ones in the study read.12
